blocks.text: To the Nabataean realms, that is, into Arabia, where the Nabataean Arabs live, descended from Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael, Gen. XXV, 13. The Israelites were in those places at that time. [II, 662] Thus in Exod. X, 19 it is not the east wind that drives the locusts from Egypt into the Red Sea, but another wind, contrary to it, namely the west wind. For Moses says: The Lord sent a very strong west wind, which carried off those locusts and cast them into the Red Sea. This same wind, then, ought to have carried the quails from Egypt across the Red Sea into Arabia, not the east wind, as the Psalm has it. This objection seems easy to meet from Jerome's version, which reads: He took away the east wind from heaven, and brought in by his strength the south-west wind (Africus). As if, when the one was removed, the other was brought in. The version of the Greeks and of the Vulgate translator is the same, except that instead of the east wind they have Νότον [Noton], the south wind. For the Greeks read: Ἀπῆρεν Νότον ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ἐπήγαγεν ἐν τῇ δυναστείᾳ αὐτοῦ Λίβα [Apēren Noton ex ouranou, kai epēgagen en tē dynasteia autou Liba]. And the Vulgate translator: He removed the south wind from heaven, and brought in by his power the south-west wind. Thus in their view the Hebrew word יסע should be rendered ἀπῆρεν [apēren], he removed or he took away. If this version is accepted, there will be no objection left. Nor will it seem easy to reject, both because it has weighty authorities and because the verb הסיע, from which יסע comes, frequently occurs in the sense of removing and taking away. For it is the Hiphil of the verb נסע, which means to set out, whether from a place or to a place. So in the Hiphil הסיע is to cause someone to set out either from a place or to a place. And said of a wind, it can mean that the wind is taken away as well as that it is sent in. Yet there are, as I at least think, compelling reasons why יסע cannot be taken in this passage in the sense of taking away. First, the Psalmist borrows this יסע from Moses, whose words are, Num. XI, 31. And a wind from the Lord נסע went forth, and brought quails across from the sea. Thus, just as in Moses נסע does not mean that the wind withdrew but that it advanced to bring the quails, so in the Psalmist יסע, which is the Hiphil of the same verb, does not mean that the wind was removed but that it was sent in to bring the quails. Second, ἀπῆρεν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ [apēren ex ouranou], he took away from heaven, would in Hebrew be יסע מן השמים. But the text has בשמים, which means in heaven or into heaven, not from heaven. Accordingly יסע there is not to take away but to bring in and to send in. For as a thing is taken away from a place, so it is brought into a place. Third, to what purpose would it be said, as in Jerome, He took away the east wind and brought in the south-west wind, and in the Greek version, Ἀπῆρεν Νότον, καὶ ἐπήγαγεν Λίβα [Apēren Noton, kai epēgagen Liba], He took away the south wind, and brought in the south-west wind, since these winds are not contrary and can stand and blow at the same time? Hence the greatest Poet:
Together rush Eurus and Notus, and, thick with storms, Africus. — — — — — —
Ὡς δ᾽ Εὖρός τε Νότος τ᾽ ἐριδαίνετον ἀλλήλοιϊν· [Hōs d' Euros te Notos t' eridaineton allēloiin]
